title: 3NF
description: Understand third normal form through candidate keys, transitive dependencies, lossless decomposition, and a worked mentor assignment design.

questions.question_text: Course has CourseID as its only candidate key, CourseID → CourseName, InstructorID and InstructorID → InstructorName, InstructorOffice. Why is it in 2NF but not 3NF?
options: Because CourseID is not unique
InstructorName and InstructorOffice depend on the nonkey determinant InstructorID
Because it has too many columns
Because CourseName is nullable
questions.explanation: The single attribute key avoids partial dependencies, but InstructorID is not a superkey and its dependent name and office are nonprime.

questions.question_text: For Course(CourseID, CourseName, InstructorID, InstructorName, InstructorOffice), with CourseID → CourseName, InstructorID and InstructorID → InstructorName, InstructorOffice, which decomposition removes the instructor detail dependency?
options: Merging Course and Enrollment into one table
Instructor(InstructorID, InstructorName, InstructorOffice) and Course(CourseID, CourseName, InstructorID), referencing Instructor
Removing InstructorID from Course entirely with no replacement
Adding a composite key of CourseID and InstructorID to Course
questions.explanation: The office and name belong under InstructorID; course identity and its instructor reference remain under CourseID.

questions.question_text: In the formal 3NF condition 'for every FD X -> Y, X is a superkey OR Y consists only of prime attributes, ' what is the second clause specifically meant to permit?
options: Any transitive dependency whatsoever
Certain FDs to a prime (candidate-key-participating) attribute to be allowed even when X is not a superkey, avoiding unnecessary over-decomposition in schemas with overlapping candidate keys
Composite keys to be split into single attributes
All non-key attributes to be treated as if they were keys
questions.explanation: This escape clause is precisely what 3NF relaxes compared to BCNF — it tolerates certain dependencies into prime attributes that BCNF would still flag as violations.

questions.question_text: Instructor(InstructorID, Name, Office) exists independently, and Course references it. Can a new instructor with no assigned course be recorded?
options: It is still impossible, since Course requires an InstructorID
Yes, insert one Instructor row without requiring a Course or Enrollment row
He must first be added as a placeholder student
He can only be added by an administrator with special privileges
questions.explanation: The independent Instructor relation stores the instructor fact before any course assignment exists.

questions.question_text: Why can a dependency-preserving 3NF design be useful when choosing between 3NF and BCNF decompositions?
options: Because it is the only normal form that actually exists in practice
3NF synthesis can preserve dependencies locally, while a BCNF decomposition may lose dependency preservation
Because SQL databases cannot enforce normal forms beyond 3NF
Because 3NF requires fewer tables than 1NF
questions.explanation: The trade off is constraint preservation; 3NF does not universally eliminate every possible anomaly, and stricter normal forms are not merely rare exceptions.

questions.question_text: Each current office is stored once in Instructor(InstructorID, Name, Office), keyed by InstructorID. How many rows must change when one instructor moves?
options: One row in Instructor
Three rows, one per course he teaches
Zero rows, since offices cannot be changed
All rows in the Enrollment table
questions.explanation: The office fact has one authoritative row for the specified instructor under this declared design.

questions.question_text: Student, Course, and Instructor facts are stored independently, with Enrollment storing only their relationship. What happens to the previously illustrated anomalies caused by repeating those independent facts in Enrollment?
options: All three anomalies (insertion, update, deletion) from 21.2-21.4 still remain
Those specific insertion, update, and deletion anomalies are removed by this declared decomposition
Only the deletion anomaly remains
Only the insertion anomaly remains
questions.explanation: The claim concerns the specified duplicated student, course, and instructor facts; it is not a universal assertion that every 3NF design has no anomalies.

questions.question_text: In Course(CourseID, CourseName, InstructorID, InstructorName, InstructorOffice), CourseID is the only candidate key and an instructor can teach many courses. If InstructorID determines only instructor name and office, is InstructorID a superkey?
options: Yes, because it determines InstructorName and InstructorOffice
No, it does not determine CourseID or CourseName
Yes, because it is a foreign key
No, because InstructorID is never functionally dependent on anything
questions.explanation: Its closure lacks course identity and course name, so InstructorID does not determine every attribute.

questions.question_text: Which fact establishes a functional dependency in a design?
options: A rule holding in every valid state
Three coincidentally matching sample rows
The physical ordering of rows
The name of a column
questions.explanation: Functional dependencies express constraints over valid states, not accidental sample patterns.

questions.question_text: In Assignment(student, mentor, office), student determines mentor and mentor determines office. Why split it?
options: Every table must have two columns
Office depends on a nonkey mentor determinant
All foreign keys violate 3NF
A single column key violates 2NF
questions.explanation: Mentor is not a superkey and office is nonprime under the stated rules.

questions.question_text: What is a prime attribute?
options: Only the first primary key column
An attribute belonging to any candidate key
Any integer column
Any foreign key column
questions.explanation: Prime membership considers every candidate key.

questions.question_text: For each nontrivial X → A, which condition permits 3NF?
options: X must always be a single column
A must always be nonprime
X is a superkey or A is prime
X must be a foreign key
questions.explanation: The formal 3NF rule includes the prime attribute alternative.

questions.question_text: Does adding a surrogate identifier remove instructor → course?
options: Yes, all dependencies disappear
Yes, if its type is integer
Only if rows are sorted
No, the business dependency remains
questions.explanation: A new identifier does not alter the original business rule.

questions.question_text: Why is the mentor decomposition lossless?
options: The common mentor identifier is a key of MentorOffice
The tables have equal row counts
Both names contain mentor
There are exactly two tables
questions.explanation: A common attribute determining one side supports the binary lossless join test.

questions.question_text: What does dependency preservation allow?
options: Avoiding every join query forever
Checking original dependencies locally in decomposed relations
Removing all foreign keys
Guaranteeing faster reads
questions.explanation: Preservation concerns constraint enforcement without joining the pieces.

questions.question_text: For R(A, B, C) with AB → C and C → B, which pair is also a candidate key?
options: BC
B alone
AC
C alone
questions.explanation: AC determines B through C, so it determines all attributes and is minimal.

questions.question_text: Why can R(A, B, C), AB → C and C → B, be 3NF but fail BCNF?
options: B is nonprime while C is a superkey
3NF forbids all composite keys
BCNF permits only one key
B is prime while C is not a superkey
questions.explanation: The prime attribute exception admits C → B in 3NF.

questions.question_text: What should a synthesis procedure add if no generated relation contains an original candidate key?
options: A relation containing a candidate key
A duplicate of every relation
A nullable office field everywhere
A random single attribute table
questions.explanation: A key relation is part of the classical synthesis lossless guarantee.

questions.question_text: Which assumption would invalidate mentor_id → current_office?
options: Several students share a mentor
One mentor can have several current offices
An office name contains spaces
The mentor identifier is indexed
questions.explanation: Multiple current office values for one mentor contradict the dependency.

questions.question_text: What should happen before declaring a normalized schema ready?
options: Assume sample uniqueness proves all keys
Delete all reporting views
Check dependencies, reconstruction, and business scenarios
Remove every repeated identifier
questions.explanation: Normal form classification is only one part of a correct schema design.

original_questions.question_text: Why is Course(CourseID, CourseName, InstructorID, InstructorName, InstructorOffice) NOT in 3NF, even though it is in 2NF?
options: Because CourseID is not unique
Because InstructorName and InstructorOffice are transitively dependent on CourseID via the non-key attribute InstructorID
Because it has too many columns
Because CourseName is nullable
original_questions.explanation: 2NF only rules out partial dependency; the transitive chain CourseID -> InstructorID -> InstructorOffice remains, which specifically violates 3NF.

original_questions.question_text: Which decomposition brings the Course relation into 3NF?
options: Merging Course and Enrollment into one table
Splitting out Instructor(InstructorID, InstructorName, InstructorOffice), leaving Course(CourseID, CourseName, InstructorID) as a foreign key reference
Removing InstructorID from Course entirely with no replacement
Adding a composite key of CourseID and InstructorID to Course
original_questions.explanation: Relocating InstructorName/InstructorOffice into their own Instructor relation, keyed directly by InstructorID, removes the transitive chain from Course.

original_questions.question_text: In the formal 3NF condition 'for every FD X -> Y, X is a superkey OR Y consists only of prime attributes,' what is the second clause specifically meant to permit?
options: Any transitive dependency whatsoever
Certain FDs to a prime (candidate-key-participating) attribute to be allowed even when X is not a superkey, avoiding unnecessary over-decomposition in schemas with overlapping candidate keys
Composite keys to be split into single attributes
All non-key attributes to be treated as if they were keys
original_questions.explanation: This escape clause is precisely what 3NF relaxes compared to BCNF — it tolerates certain dependencies into prime attributes that BCNF would still flag as violations.

original_questions.question_text: After achieving 3NF with the final schema (Student, Instructor, Course, Enrollment), what happens when Dr. Fernandez (a new instructor with no assigned course yet) needs to be recorded?
options: It is still impossible, since Course requires an InstructorID
He can be inserted directly into the Instructor table with no dependency on any Course or Enrollment row — the insertion anomaly is resolved
He must first be added as a placeholder student
He can only be added by an administrator with special privileges
original_questions.explanation: Since Instructor is now its own independent relation keyed by InstructorID, a new instructor can be recorded with zero need for a course or enrollment to exist first.

original_questions.question_text: Why is 3NF often considered 'good enough' for most real-world production schemas?
options: Because it is the only normal form that actually exists in practice
Because it eliminates all three classic anomalies (insertion, update, deletion) while staying practical to query, whereas BCNF/4NF/5NF address increasingly rare edge cases
Because SQL databases cannot enforce normal forms beyond 3NF
Because 3NF requires fewer tables than 1NF
original_questions.explanation: 3NF resolves the anomalies that matter for everyday design; the stricter forms close narrower, less commonly encountered loopholes at the cost of more fragmented schemas.

original_questions.question_text: In the fully 3NF-normalized schema, updating Dr. Rao's office requires touching how many rows?
options: One row, in the Instructor table
Three rows, one per course he teaches
Zero rows, since offices cannot be changed
All rows in the Enrollment table
original_questions.explanation: Because InstructorOffice now lives in a single Instructor row keyed by InstructorID, exactly one row needs to change — the update anomaly is fully resolved.

original_questions.question_text: Which of the following anomalies, if any, still remains after reaching the 3NF schema described (Student, Instructor, Course, Enrollment)?
options: All three anomalies (insertion, update, deletion) from 21.2-21.4 still remain
None of the three classic anomalies from 21.2-21.4 remain for this schema
Only the deletion anomaly remains
Only the insertion anomaly remains
original_questions.explanation: The full decomposition through 2NF and 3NF resolves the insertion, update, and deletion anomalies illustrated earlier in the chapter for this particular table's dependency structure.

original_questions.question_text: Is InstructorID a superkey of the pre-decomposition Course(CourseID, CourseName, InstructorID, InstructorName, InstructorOffice) relation?
options: Yes, because it determines InstructorName and InstructorOffice
No — its closure only reaches {InstructorID, InstructorName, InstructorOffice}, never CourseID or CourseName, so it does not determine every attribute of Course
Yes, because it is a foreign key
No, because InstructorID is never functionally dependent on anything
original_questions.explanation: A superkey's closure must reach every attribute of the relation. InstructorID never determines CourseID/CourseName (an instructor can teach multiple courses), so it fails as a superkey — confirming the transitive dependency is a genuine 3NF violation.

coding_not_applicable: Schema design and dependency proofs require evaluating keys, lossless joins, and constraint preservation; a single SQL result judge cannot establish these properties. Three worked design exercises and solutions are included.

notes:
## Why third normal form matters

A placement office records each student's assigned mentor and the mentor's office. If the same mentor serves forty students, storing the office on every assignment repeats one fact forty times. Changing the office can leave contradictory rows; deleting the last student assignment can erase the only record of that office. Third normal form, abbreviated 3NF, helps place each fact under the determinant that actually identifies it. It is a logical design rule, rather than a promise that every query becomes faster or every kind of duplication disappears.

A functional dependency X → Y means that any two valid rows agreeing on X must agree on Y. This is a rule of the modeled world, not a pattern inferred safely from three sample rows. A candidate key is a minimal set of attributes determining every attribute. A superkey also determines everything, but may contain unnecessary attributes. A prime attribute belongs to at least one candidate key. The chosen SQL primary key is only one candidate key and cannot replace reasoning about the others.

## State the rule precisely

For every nontrivial dependency X → A implied by the dependency set, a relation is in 3NF when X is a superkey or A is prime. A dependency is trivial when its right side is already contained in its left side. The prime attribute alternative matters when candidate keys overlap. The familiar phrase about removing transitive dependencies between nonkey facts is a useful introduction, but the formal test handles cases that phrase can obscure.

For a beginner example, use Assignment(student_id, mentor_id, office). Assume each student has exactly one mentor and each mentor has exactly one current office. Then student_id determines mentor_id, and mentor_id determines office. Student_id is the only candidate key under these assumptions. Mentor_id is not a superkey because several students can share it. Office is nonprime. The dependency mentor_id → office therefore violates 3NF even though the relation has a single attribute key and has no partial key dependency.

## Work through the decomposition

Split the relation into StudentMentor(student_id, mentor_id) and MentorOffice(mentor_id, office). StudentMentor stores the assignment; MentorOffice stores the office fact. The repeated mentor identifier is intentional because it connects facts. What disappears is the repeated claim about that mentor's office. Both relations are in 3NF under the declared dependencies. Each nontrivial determinant in either relation is a key of that relation.

```sql
CREATE TABLE mentor_office (
  mentor_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
  office VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL
);
CREATE TABLE student_mentor (
  student_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
  mentor_id INT NOT NULL,
  FOREIGN KEY (mentor_id) REFERENCES mentor_office(mentor_id)
);
INSERT INTO mentor_office VALUES (7, 'North 204'), (9, 'West 110');
INSERT INTO student_mentor VALUES (101, 7), (102, 7), (103, 9);
SELECT s.student_id, s.mentor_id, m.office
FROM student_mentor AS s
JOIN mentor_office AS m ON m.mentor_id = s.mentor_id
ORDER BY s.student_id;
```

The result is three rows: student 101 and student 102 each show mentor 7 and North 204; student 103 shows mentor 9 and West 110. Updating mentor 7's office now changes one authoritative row. The join reconstructs the original information without inventing combinations because the shared mentor identifier is a key of MentorOffice. This is the lossless join property, which must be justified separately from merely naming a normal form.

## Preserve the rules as well as the rows

Dependency preservation means that the original functional dependencies can be enforced through constraints on the decomposed relations without joining them to detect a violation. Here student_id → mentor_id is local to StudentMentor, and mentor_id → office is local to MentorOffice. The foreign key guarantees that a referenced mentor exists; it does not itself prove normalization or enforce every business rule. For example, these tables allow a mentor with no students, which is useful for recording a newly hired mentor before an assignment exists.

The classical 3NF synthesis approach begins with a minimal cover of dependencies. Split right sides, remove extraneous left attributes, and remove redundant dependencies while preserving the same closure. Form relations containing each determinant and its dependent attributes, combine suitable relations, and remove contained relations. If no resulting relation contains a candidate key of the original schema, include a key relation. The key relation is essential to the lossless guarantee; arbitrary splitting can lose information even if individual pieces look tidy.

## Candidate keys can change the diagnosis

Consider Teaching(student, course, instructor), with student and course together determining instructor, and instructor determining course. Assume these are the complete rules. Student plus course is a candidate key; student plus instructor is another. All three attributes are therefore prime. Instructor → course has a determinant that is not a superkey, but its right side is prime, so this relation satisfies 3NF. It fails the stricter BCNF condition, which requires a superkey determinant for every nontrivial dependency.

This example explains why 3NF and BCNF should not be treated as interchangeable labels. A decomposition into stronger normal forms can make some dependencies harder to enforce locally. A design choice should identify which constraints remain enforceable and how the application protects the others. Adding a surrogate row identifier does not remove an existing dependency between instructor and course; the business dependencies survive even when the table receives a convenient technical primary key.

## Recognize design mistakes

Do not declare a dependency merely because the current data happens to have unique office names. Two mentors might share a room tomorrow. Ask whether the business prohibits that state. Similarly, an office may be historical rather than current: if mentors can move, a dated assignment needs a time dimension and a different dependency analysis. Normalization is always relative to the stated meaning of a row. A poorly chosen row meaning cannot be repaired by mechanically splitting column names.

Do not confuse a database constraint with a discovered fact. A unique constraint may implement a candidate key once nullability and domain requirements are settled, but leaving a constraint absent does not make the logical dependency disappear. Conversely, SQL nulls and duplicate rows need explicit implementation decisions because classical relational reasoning assumes set semantics and ordinary attribute values. Use clear NOT NULL constraints for mandatory keys and document optional relationships instead of treating missing values as ordinary identifiers.

## Exercises with explained solutions

Exercise one: Shipment(shipment_id, depot_id, depot_phone) has shipment_id → depot_id and depot_id → depot_phone. Identify the violation and propose relations. The answer is that depot_id is not a shipment key while depot_phone is nonprime. Use Shipment(shipment_id, depot_id) and Depot(depot_id, depot_phone). Their common attribute is a key of Depot, giving a lossless reconstruction. Updating one depot phone no longer requires rewriting every shipment handled by that depot.

Exercise two: R(A, B, C) has AB → C and C → B. Find candidate keys before classifying it. AB determines all attributes. AC also determines all attributes because C supplies B. Neither A, B, nor C alone determines everything. Every attribute is prime, so C → B is permitted by 3NF even though C is not a superkey. The relation is therefore in 3NF but not BCNF. This reasoning depends on the declared dependency set, not an attractive sample table.

Exercise three: someone splits Assignment into StudentMentor(student_id, mentor_id) and StudentOffice(student_id, office). Is the original mentor office rule locally preserved? No. Both new tables use the student identifier, so checking that every student of mentor 7 has the same office requires comparing assignments across the join. The split may reconstruct rows, yet it misses the desired ownership of the office fact. Evaluate dependency preservation and losslessness independently rather than assuming either follows from having two primary keys.

Before implementation, list candidate keys, justify each dependency, and describe insertion, update, and deletion scenarios. Then inspect actual query needs and add indexes where measurements justify them. Normalized writes can coexist with derived reporting views, provided the source of truth remains clear. Continue with [BCNF](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/bcnf) to study stronger determinant requirements, and revisit [2NF](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/2nf) when a composite key creates partial dependencies.
